abstract: TPNC-NZTD: TOPOLOGICAL PHOTONIC NEUROMORPHIC COMPUTING WITH NEAR-ZERO THERMAL DISSIPATION Author: Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-RakhawiDOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23337933 A revolutionary hybrid chip architecture solving AI's energy crisis by integrating three Nobel Prize-winning phenomena: photonic computing (light instead of electrons), topological insulators (backscattering-immune edge states), and spiking neural networks (event-driven computation). Core architecture: 2D topological insulator substrate (bismuthene on SiC) + nanoscale photonic waveguides along edges + non-linear optical synapses (phase-change materials GeSbTe or 2D TMDs) + photonic neurons with thresholding behavior. Quantum-limited performance: Energy per photon at 1550 nm = 0.128 aJ. With 10-100 photons per spike for reliable detection above noise floor: E_spike = 10-100 aJ (100-1000× improvement over electronic SNNs). Thermal dissipation: 10 aJ × 1 MHz × 10⁶ synapses = 10 μW per million synapses (1,000,000× improvement over electronic chips). Computational speed: 100 GHz - 1 THz via photonic propagation. Fabrication: CMOS BEOL-compatible via heterogeneous integration (micro-transfer printing or adhesive wafer bonding of III-V materials), preserving topological bandgap integrity during processing. Applications: Edge AI/IoT ($50B), data center acceleration ($150B), autonomous systems ($30B), scientific computing ($20B), neuromorphic research ($5B). Total addressable market: $300B+ by 2030. Comprehensive IP protection: 5 patent claims covering hybrid architecture, photonic spike computation method, heterogeneous fabrication process preserving topological states, synaptic weight update protocols, and application-specific deployments. Trade secrets, perpetual moral rights under Berne Convention, 4 protected trademarks. All rights reserved, proprietary. Full citation: El-Rakhawi, M. K. A. (2026). abstract: Many optimization problems provide direct access to only part of the gradient, while the remaining component must be inferred from function evaluations. This structure arises in performative prediction, performative reinforcement learning, and bilevel optimization with a black-box lower level. We introduce Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization (PISO), which combines the available gradient component with a running estimate of the residual. By centring each zeroth-order observation on this estimate, PISO makes the variance due to random probing depend on the tracking error rather than the residual's magnitude. This yields a randomized sketch iteration with an explicit contraction mechanism and a principled interpretation of momentum. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence guarantees that depend on the residual's variation and initial magnitude, without requiring a uniform bound on the unavailable gradient component. With independently sampled function evaluations and Gaussian or spherical probes, PISO attains leading function-evaluation complexities of \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-6})\) under Lipschitz gradients and \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-5})\) under an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption. These rates require only one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-component sample per update. The analysis also quantifies how batching trades observations for fewer deployments. Across five settings, PISO variants improve on the tested baselines with comparable oracle access in three, reach a comparable solution faster in bilevel routing, and perform best among methods without response-model derivatives in performative reinforcement learning.
title: Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization via Zeroth-Order Residual Tracking

abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.
title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
